W0012.text:
Characterization of the subthalamo-cortical pathway and its involvement in the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease
This thesis investigated the role of the STN in pain symptoms associated with Parkinson's disease and provided an anatomo-functional characterization of the STN-M1 pathway under normal and parkinsonian conditions using chemogenetic, optogenetic, behavioral, and electrophysiological approaches in Vglut2-cre mice. Our results showed that selective inhibition of glutamatergic neurons in the STN improves motor and nociceptive deficits induced by 6-OHDA dopaminergic lesions. Anatomical analyses revealed the existence of direct projections from the STN to the motor and somatosensory cortices in mice, with preferential connectivity to PV+ cortical interneurons in the M1 cortex. Optogenetic inhibition of the STN-M1 pathway attenuated motor and pain-related alterations and restored disrupted nociceptive cortical responses under parkinsonian conditions. These results identify the STN-M1 pathway as a major player in the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease and highlight its therapeutic potential.

W0144.text: Role of Arkypallidal neurons in motor symptoms of Parkinson's Disease and L-DOPA-induced-dyskinesia: study in a rodent model. The external Globus Pallidus (GPe) is a central structure within the basal ganglia, primarily involved in information transmission via the indirect pathway. It is composed mainly of GABAergic neurons, divided into two subtypes: prototypic neurons and arkypallidal (ARKY) neurons, which are distinguished by their molecular and electrophysiological signatures. Our team recently demonstrated that optogenetic activation of ARKY neurons suppresses ongoing action, suggesting a key role in movement control. Parkinson's Disease (PD), the second most common neurodegenerative disorder worldwide, is characterized by severe motor impairments. Although L-DOPA-based dopaminergic replacement therapy initially relieves symptoms, its long-term use often leads to involuntary movements known as L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID). Despite extensive research on PD and LID, the role of ARKY neurons in these conditions remains poorly understood. The objective of my PhD was therefore to investigate functional modifications of ARKY neurons in mouse models of PD and LID using multidisciplinary approaches. My work revealed that ARKY neuron activity is altered in mouse models of PD and LID. I demonstrated that the intrinsic excitability of ARKY neurons is modified in PD and LID, and that ARKY neuron projections to the striatum are increased in both pathophysiological conditions. Furthermore, I showed that ARKY neurons are inhibited by L-DOPA in acute brain slices, suggesting that L-DOPA exerts its dyskinetic effects partly by acting in the GPe.

W0222.text:
Study of the network involving the subthalamic nucleus in various measures of motivation in the rat

The subthalamic nucleus (STN), a nucleus of the basal ganglia, is the target of deep brain stimulation (DBS) for the treatment of Parkinson's disease. Work from our laboratory has shown that STN inactivation, by lesion or DBS, reduces motivation for cocaine while increasing motivation for sugar. STN modulation can prevent addiction-related features, such as loss of control over consumption and compulsive drug seeking. These results highlighted the role of the STN in motivational processes and supported our proposal of STN DBS as a surgical treatment for addiction. The aim of this thesis was to clarify the role of the STN and to identify which of its neural networks is involved in motivated behaviors. Since STN inhibition reduces drug intake and affective responses, the STN may be involved in "liking," "wanting," or both. It has been reported that some Parkinson's patients can self-stimulate via DBS, raising questions about the role of the STN in intracranial self-stimulation (ICSS). The first part of this thesis therefore investigated whether STN stimulation could generate ICSS. To test this hypothesis, we used electrical DBS and optogenetics. Rats implanted with electrodes in the STN could self-administer stimulation at three different frequencies (8, 30, 130 Hz). Concurrently, other rats infected with excitatory, inhibitory, or control opsins in the STN could self-administer light pulses. The results showed that 130 Hz STN DBS and optogenetic inhibition increased ICSS, suggesting that the STN must be inhibited to generate ICSS, which may be related to pleasure but also to the reinforcing aspect of rewards. These reward-related effects are not limited to the STN. The final part of this thesis aimed to identify the involved brain network. The STN receives direct cortical projections (hyperdirect pathway), and the role of this pathway in the motivational effects of STN manipulations needs to be understood. We used calcium imaging (fiber photometry) to observe the activity dynamics of this pathway during a sucrose motivation test. A Progressive Ratio (PR) protocol was used to measure the motivation to exert effort to obtain sucrose. The infralimbic (IL), prelimbic (PL), and anterior cingulate (ACg) cortices were targeted with a Cre-dependent Genetically Encoded Calcium Indicator (GECI) virus, while Cav2-Cre was injected into the STN for retrograde labeling. Optical fibers were implanted above the STN to record calcium activity in cortico-STN terminals during behavior. The results show differential activity among the hyperdirect pathways. The IL-STN and ACg-STN pathways show increased activity upon reward delivery in the PR task. In contrast, STN neuron activity shows increased calcium signals during reward consumption. These results suggest that hyperdirect pathways from the IL and ACg are involved in reward-seeking behavior, whereas the STN is more engaged in reward consumption and the evaluation of its incentive value. In a final experiment, the IL-STN, ACg-STN, and PL-STN pathways were selectively inhibited using optogenetics during the PR task. Inhibition of each hyperdirect pathway decreased motivation for sugar. Overall, these results highlight the critical and distinct roles of the STN and the hyperdirect pathway in motivation and reward consumption. They provide additional evidence that STN manipulation may be a promising strategy for treating addiction.

W0267.text: Role of neuronal subpopulations of the external globus pallidus in the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease: Optogenetic and behavioral study in the mouse model. The external globus pallidus (GPe) is part of the basal ganglia (BG), a set of interconnected subcortical structures that, together with the cortex and thalamus, form a highly organized and complex network involved in the control of voluntary motor activity. The GPe has long been considered a simple relay structure within the BG, but recent studies have revealed a diversity of neuronal populations and anatomical connections, suggesting that it rather plays a role as an integrative center. GABAergic neurons of the GPe have been subdivided into two major subpopulations: arkypallidal neurons, which exclusively innervate the striatum, and prototypic neurons, which innervate all BG structures. This doctoral work, conducted in the mouse model, aims to clarify the functional role of the GPe, and more specifically of its neuronal subpopulations, under physiological and pathological conditions associated with Parkinson's disease (PD). In a first part, we studied the behavioral effects of optogenetic manipulation of GPe activity in mice. Optogenetic inactivation of the GPe had no effect on spontaneous locomotor activity. In contrast, it altered exploratory behavior directed toward salient elements of the environment and improved spatial working memory performance, revealing that the GPe is engaged in motor and cognitive processes in a manner that closely depends on the behavioral task implemented. We then examined the effects of optogenetic activation of the GPe on motor deficits induced by unilateral lesion of the nigrostriatal dopaminergic pathway, the standard mouse model of PD. GPe activation improved all motor deficits studied (locomotor asymmetry, forelimb akinesia, and locomotor hypoactivity). These data highlight the importance of the GPe in the development of PD motor disorders. In a second part, we used transgenic mouse lines to selectively target arkypallidal (molecular marker: FoxP2 protein) and prototypic neurons to elucidate their respective functional roles. For prototypic neurons, we targeted those expressing parvalbumin (PV), which represent the majority fraction and primarily innervate the subthalamic nucleus and the output structures of the BG. Unilateral optogenetic activation of FoxP2 or PV neurons induced contralateral rotations in mice, similar to global unilateral GPe activation. We then verified whether activation of these neurons reduced the motor deficits induced by dopaminergic lesion. Photostimulation of FoxP2 and PV neurons improved the locomotor asymmetry deficit in lesioned mice, but only PV neuron activation proved effective in correcting forelimb akinesia. These data show that FoxP2 and PV neurons of the GPe similarly influence certain aspects of locomotor behavior by acting on distinct BG structures. They further suggest that PV neuron dysfunction plays a central role in the manifestation of PD motor disorders. Collectively, these studies provide new insights into the functional role of the GPe and its involvement in the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease. The beneficial effects obtained through manipulation of this nucleus's activity open interesting research perspectives for the development of new PD therapies based on optogenetic neuromodulation.

W0378.text: Cerebellar stimulation prevents levodopa-induced dyskinesia in mice and normalizes brain activity. Theta-burst cerebellar stimulation prevents the onset of levodopa-induced dyskinesia and normalizes brain activity. Chronic levodopa therapy, the standard treatment for Parkinson's disease (PD), leads to the emergence of painful, involuntary abnormal movements known as levodopa-induced dyskinesia (LID). Cerebellar stimulation has been shown to reduce the severity of LID in dyskinetic patients. However, the underlying mechanisms and the neural circuits involved in this effect remain unknown. In this study, we used a murine model of LID and a genetically modified mouse line enabling the optogenetic activation of a specific neuronal population in the cerebellar cortex: Purkinje cells (PCs), to determine how cerebellar stimulation alleviates LID. Accordingly, we applied short trains of optogenetic stimulation, in the theta frequency range, to PCs in awake, freely moving mice. We demonstrated that these stimulations are sufficient to reduce the severity of LID and even prevent its onset when stimulation begins concurrently with levodopa treatment. This symptomatic relief is accompanied by a normalization of aberrant neuronal activity in the deep cerebellar nuclei, the motor cortex, and the parafascicular nucleus of the thalamus. Specific inhibition of the cerebello-parafascicular pathway counteracts the beneficial effects of cerebellar stimulation. Furthermore, cerebellar stimulation reverses the sign of plasticity at corticostriatal synapses of striatonigral neurons and normalizes the aberrant overexpression of FosB/ΔFosB, a well-known transcription factor causally linked to LID. These results demonstrate that the alleviation and prevention of LID by daily PC stimulation are accompanied by the restoration of function in a broad brain network and are capable of restoring deep, intrinsic alterations in the striatum associated with LID.

W0428.text: Study of dopaminergic neurons and brainstem locomotor circuits in a mouse model of Parkinson’s disease. Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative pathology characterized by severe locomotor deficits due to the degeneration of meso-diencephalic dopaminergic neurons. These neurons modulate several brain structures involved in movement programming, including the Mesencephalic Locomotor Region (MLR). This brainstem region controls locomotion initiation and locomotor speed in vertebrates. When dopaminergic neurons die, MLR activity decreases, which may contribute to locomotor deficits. To date, the vulnerability factors of dopaminergic neurons in PD are not yet well defined, but studies suggest that neurons using glutamate as a co-transmitter during their development may be more vulnerable. However, no comparison has been made with neurons that do not degenerate in PD. Regarding PD treatments, approaches based on L-DOPA administration or deep brain stimulation of the basal ganglia suggest that the beneficial effects on locomotor function may involve an increase in MLR activity. Yet, MLR stimulation has never been studied in an animal model of PD. Current treatments lose efficacy as the pathology progresses, highlighting the importance of finding new therapeutic targets to improve locomotor function in PD. The first objective of my doctoral work was to compare the expression of a gene characteristic of the glutamatergic phenotype, the vesicular glutamate transporter type 2 (Vglut2), in dopaminergic nuclei A8-A13 using a cell fate mapping technique in mice. My work shows that dopaminergic nuclei known to degenerate in PD express Vglut2 at some point in their life, unlike those that do not degenerate. The second objective was to study in vivo the effects of MLR stimulation on locomotor deficits induced in a mouse model of PD based on intracerebral injection of a neurotoxin. My work shows that optogenetic stimulation of glutamatergic neurons (Vglut2+) in the cuneiform nucleus, the dorsal part of the MLR, increases the number of locomotor initiations and locomotor speed, while inducing locomotor movements very close to those spontaneously exhibited by intact animals. Thus, my doctoral work has improved our understanding of the diversity of dopaminergic nuclei, highlighted a factor potentially associated with the vulnerability of DA neurons in PD, and proposed a new potential clinical target to improve locomotor function in PD.

W0454.text: Contribution of striatal cholinergic interneurons to cognitive deficits in Parkinson's disease: optogenetic and behavioral approaches in mice. Parkinson's disease (PD) is primarily characterized by motor symptoms, but also includes psychiatric and cognitive disorders. PD is caused by the progressive loss of dopaminergic (DA) neurons projecting to the striatum. Within this structure, DA neurons interact with cholinergic interneurons (CINs) to modulate certain motor and cognitive functions. Using behavioral, lesion, and optogenetic approaches in mice, my doctoral work shows that DA neuron lesion or CIN inactivation induces impulsivity and flexibility deficits; these cognitive dysfunctions may precede the onset of motor symptoms and thus constitute early markers of the disease. However, the interaction between these two neuronal populations does not appear to be involved in the development of these specific cognitive disorders in our murine model of PD.

W0465.text:
Electrophysiological characterization of neuronal diversity in the substantia nigra pars reticulata in control and parkinsonian mice

The substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) is the main output structure of the basal ganglia (BG), a subcortical network controlling the elaboration of motor programs as well as cognitive and associative learning functions. The identification of distinct cell types in the BG has played a key role in understanding the properties and functions of this circuit. Recent studies suggest that the SNr is composed of multiple cell types, but to date this neuronal diversity has never been considered regarding the normal and pathological functioning of this nucleus, particularly in Parkinson's disease (PD). By combining immunohistochemical and electrophysiological approaches in the PVCre::Ai9T mouse line, we demonstrated that parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) SNr neurons have different anatomical and electrophysiological properties than non-expressing neurons (PV-). Our anatomical analysis shows that PV+ and PV- neurons are present in equal proportions in the SNr, but with a distinct distribution, PV+ neurons being enriched in the lateral part of the SNr while PV- neurons are present in the medial part of this nucleus. Our in vitro electrophysiological recordings revealed that PV+ neurons have higher electrical activity than PV- cells. Furthermore, our data indicate that dopamine (DA) loss and L-DOPA treatment induce a profound reduction in the excitability of PV+ SNr neurons in a murine model of PD (the 6-OHDA mouse) without altering the activity of PV- neurons. It is well known that the activity of SNr neurons is controlled by GABAergic afferents from striatal neurons (STR-SNr) of the direct pathway (dSPN) and the globus pallidus (GP-SNr). We performed optogenetic manipulation of these two inhibitory pathways and showed that these two neuronal populations are innervated equivalently by the STR and the GP. Our results also revealed that striatal inhibition was more effective than pallidal inhibition in reducing the activity of both SNr neuron subtypes. Moreover, we observed that the STR-SNr and GP-SNr synapses display the same short-term plasticity on PV+ and PV- SNr neurons. Finally, we showed that GABAergic transmission is differentially affected on PV+ and PV- cells following DA depletion. On the one hand, PV+ neurons are more sensitive to striatal inhibition than PV- cells after DA depletion. On the other hand, pallidal inhibition is reduced on PV+ neurons and increased on PV- neurons after DA loss, suggesting an imbalance of pallidal inhibition between these two SNr populations. It is also known that extracellular GABA levels are elevated in the SNr in rodent models of PD, suggesting that SNr neurons could be permanently inhibited by so-called tonic inhibition. Thus, we characterized extrasynaptic GABAergic transmission in the SNr of control and 6-OHDA mice. Our patch-clamp recordings revealed that PV- neurons exhibit greater tonic inhibition than PV+ cells in control mice. The presence and involvement of δ and α5 subunits in extrasynaptic GABAA receptors were also studied, revealing a major presence and effect of α5 subunits on PV neurons. However, contrary to expectations, chronic DA depletion causes no change in tonic inhibition in either PV+ cells or PV- neurons of the SNr. Our results highlight the importance of differentiating SNr cell populations for a better understanding of BG functioning in physiological and pathophysiological conditions such as in PD.

W0607.text:
Ventral Hippocampus Parvalbumin Positive Interneurons Can Modulate Retrieval of Social Memory in Mice.

Social memory is crucial for the survival and reproduction of animals. Like other types of memory, the processing of social memory can be divided into three basic stages: encoding, consolidation, and retrieval. Disruptions in any of these processing stages can lead to impairments in social recognition. Studies in both animals and humans have shown that the hippocampus plays a significant role in various processing stages of episodic memory. Episodic memory comprises four well-known fundamental elements: time, place, person, and event. As an important component of episodic memory, social memory provides key information regarding the "person" and is closely linked to the hippocampus. Meanwhile, social memory impairment is a common phenotype in psychiatric disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease and autism spectrum disorder. However, despite the considerable attention given to social memory impairment in psychiatric research, few studies have explored the relationship between the specific processing stage of social memory impairment and its corresponding neuropathological mechanisms. Furthermore, research has indicated that deficits in Parvalbumin-positive interneurons (hereafter referred to as PV neurons), which are prevalent in psychiatric disorders, may be a potential cause of social memory impairment. Nevertheless, how PV neurons influence social memory and which memory processing stage they act upon remains unknown. Based on this, the present study used adeno-associated virus vectors and transgenic animals to achieve specific ablation and optogenetic manipulation of PV neurons in the mouse hippocampus, aiming to elucidate the mechanism by which PV neurons function in social memory. The findings are as follows: (1) Eight weeks of social isolation in early adolescent mice induced a reduction in PV expression in the CA1 and CA2/3 regions of the ventral hippocampus, concurrently causing social memory impairment. Further analysis revealed a significant correlation between PV counts in the ventral CA1 region (hereafter referred to as vCA1) and social memory behavioral metrics, with both exhibiting a co-variation trend during social isolation. (2) Specific ablation of two types of interneurons in vCA1—PV neurons and somatostatin-positive interneurons (hereafter referred to as SOM neurons)—showed that ablating PV neurons in this region disrupted social memory, whereas ablating SOM neurons had no effect. (3) Using optogenetic tools, activation and inhibition of vCA1 PV neurons during the retrieval stage impaired social recognition, while manipulation during the encoding and maintenance stages did not affect final social recognition. Activating PV neurons when approaching a familiar mouse caused the experimental animals to discriminate the familiar mouse as a stranger. (4) Through calcium imaging and c-Fos analysis, it was found that PV neurons exhibited higher responses when animals approached unfamiliar animals, whereas responses were weaker when approaching familiar animals. These results indicate that PV neurons in the CA1 region of the ventral hippocampus may participate in the retrieval stage of social memory, and their activation and deactivation may constitute an important neural mechanism for discriminating between novel and familiar conspecifics.

W0628.text:
Link between molecule and circuit from translational neuroimaging in neuropsychiatric disorders.
Diagnosis of psychiatric and neurological disorders has traditionally been based on clinical symptoms and neurological signs; however, in recent years, imaging techniques that directly capture molecular changes in the brain have come to play a major role. In particular, in neurological diseases, dopamine transporter imaging in Parkinson's disease and amyloid imaging in Alzheimer's disease are significantly transforming the previous symptom-centered diagnostic approach. Specifically, regarding abnormal proteins that accumulate in the brain in neurodegenerative diseases, since the development of amyloid imaging, multiple tau imaging agents have now been developed. These agents are clarifying the temporal changes in abnormal protein accumulation and the characteristic patterns of intracerebral accumulation of diverse tauopathies. Furthermore, using genetically modified animals, the relationship between tau accumulation and intracerebral inflammation or neuronal death is also becoming clearer. On the other hand, in psychiatric disorders, where there is no clear neurodegeneration or abnormal protein accumulation, imaging biomarkers that go beyond symptom assessment do not yet exist. In psychiatric disorders, the mechanisms underlying the manifestation of cardinal symptoms have not yet been fully elucidated, but it is currently assumed that there are dysfunctions in the function of neural circuits in the brain, including neurotransmitters. From this perspective, the development of animal models for psychiatric disorders requires the identification of circuits that define psychiatric symptoms. Animals, particularly primates, are suitable for evaluating higher-order functions, but circuit manipulation requires precise drug injection into local brain regions, and repeated measurements are not necessarily easy. Chemogenetic techniques (DREADD), developed in recent years, allow the control of neural activity in neurons expressing artificial receptors using the drug CNO, and the expression state in the brain can also be visualized by PET. This technique, which can transiently control specific brain neurons or neural pathways via peripherally administered drugs and thereby control behavior, even in macaques with large brains, without special devices such as optical or electrical circuits, is expected to have broad applications in validating the symptom-expression circuits and developing treatments for psychiatric and neurological disorders using primates. Elucidating the pathophysiology of psychiatric and neurological disorders and developing treatments require the acquisition of intracerebral information in vivo; however, imaging technology, particularly PET-based imaging of specific molecules, can directly visualize drug discovery targets from small animals to humans, and further expansion in future research on psychiatric and neurological disorders is expected.

W0645.text: Optogenetics-based neuromodulation for the treatment of Parkinson's disease [Powered by NICT].

W0657.text: Dynamic study of the generation of beta oscillations in Parkinson's disease. The basal ganglia (BG) form a complex loop with the cortex and thalamus that is involved in action selection and movement control. Synchronized oscillatory activities in the BG network have been proposed to play an essential role in coordinating the flow of information within these neuronal circuits. Thus, their deregulation in time and space could become pathological. In Parkinson's disease (PD), the abnormally high expression of neuronal oscillations in the beta frequency range (β, 10-30 Hz) is thought to be the cause of the motor deficits (akinetic and bradykinetic) of this disease. However, the neuronal networks underlying β oscillations and their pathophysiological involvement remain unknown. The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is an anatomical hub of the BG located at the center of networks potentially involved in the emergence of these hyper-synchronized states. The objective of this thesis was to determine the causal role of the main inputs to the STN (i.e. the motor cortex, the globus pallidus, and the parafascicular nucleus of the thalamus) in the maintenance and propagation of β oscillations. To this end, we developed optogenetic manipulation approaches combined with in vivo electrophysiological recordings in a rodent model of PD. Our work demonstrates the respective contribution of the different neuronal circuits interrogated and highlights the importance of the globus pallidus in controlling the propagation and maintenance of β oscillations throughout the BG loop.

W0661.text: Involvement of striatal cholinergic interneurons in the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease: optogenetic, pharmacological, and behavioral study. Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by dopaminergic loss in the striatum, a subcortical structure involved in motor control, memory, and emotional behaviors. Striatal cholinergic interneurons (ChIs) play a key role in this pathological reorganization of the striatum by modulating the activity of striatal projection neurons (MSNs). This work aims to investigate the involvement of ChIs and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChRs) in the mechanisms underlying the expression of motor, cognitive, and emotional deficits in different mouse models of PD. Optogenetic inhibition of ChIs reduces motor deficits (akinesia, postural asymmetry, sensorimotor deficit). Electrophysiological recordings show that ChI inhibition reduces MSN excitability and restores the balance of activity between the two striatal output pathways. These antiparkinsonian effects are reproduced by striatal pharmacological blockade of M1 and M4 mAChRs. They result from a preferential action of ACh on mAChRs at the level of MSNs originating the striatonigral pathway, as they disappear in mice with M4 receptors knocked out in these neurons. Photoinhibition of ChIs reduces memory deficits and anxiety. The M1 mAChR antagonist reduces anxiety but is ineffective on memory deficits, suggesting that other striatal cholinergic receptors may be engaged in memory functions. Taken together, our results provide new insights into the involvement of striatal ChIs in the physiological and pathological functioning of the striatum.

W0662.text: Involvement of striatonigral and striatopallidal neurons in sequential instrumental learning via optogenetic targeting. Neuronal circuits of the basal ganglia are involved in movement planning and selection, in motivational and reinforcement processes, but also in more cognitive functions such as instrumental learning processes. Dysfunction of these nuclei leads to severe motor disorders, such as Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases, and more psychiatric pathologies, including drug addiction, Gilles de la Tourette syndrome, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. The striatum, the input structure of the basal ganglia system, is composed largely of GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSN), which are subdivided into two populations: striatonigral and striatopallidal neurons. These neurons form distinct and parallel functional pathways: they originate in the striatum after receiving information from the cortex, then traverse the other basal ganglia nuclei (Globus Pallidus, Subthalamic Nucleus, Substantia Nigra), which then project to the thalamus, returning the processed information to the relevant cortical areas. These projection neurons are morphologically identical and homogeneously distributed throughout the striatum, making their specific study difficult without genetic tools. In this work, we investigated the respective roles of these two neuronal populations in sequential instrumental learning using an optogenetic approach. This technique allows for the optical, reversible control of the activity of a genetically targeted neuronal population at a physiological timescale during behavior. First, we developed mouse models in which each of these two populations is specifically targeted using the Cre/LoxP system and stereotaxic injection of viral vectors enabling the expression of light-sensitive channels, such as Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2). Validation of the functionality of this protein in these models was first established ex vivo by electrophysiological means (recording of neuronal activity in acute brain slices), then in vivo, by inducing a characteristic rotational behavior resulting from the unilateral activation of these neuronal populations. Second, these mice were studied in a behavioral paradigm linked to the dorsal striatum: sequential instrumental learning. Indeed, the execution of a sequence of actions in a well-defined order is fundamental for adopting an appropriate behavior. During the acquisition of a new sequence, each of these two neuronal populations was activated optogenetically to determine their effect on this learning. We were particularly interested in these neurons in the dorsolateral striatum (DLS), as this region plays a fundamental role in habit formation, and more specifically in sequential learning. This work highlighted the significant respective involvement of these DLS neurons during sequence acquisition, as we showed that activation of striatonigral neurons facilitated the learning of a new sequence, whereas activation of striatopallidal neurons disrupted this learning. Furthermore, our results indicate that optogenetic stimulation of striatopallidal neurons leads to a deficit in differentiating and associating actions to form a coherent unit, while activation of striatonigral neurons appears fundamental for correctly initiating and terminating a sequence. These results thus contribute to the understanding of the role of the two main pathways of the dorsolateral striatum during sequential instrumental learning.

W0680.text: Closed-loop optogenetics: an artificial loop to regulate pathological loops?

W0687.text: Processing of thalamic information through the basal ganglia: an in vivo electrophysiological and optogenetic approach. The medial/parafascicular (CM/Pf) nucleus of the thalamus has recently emerged as a key element of interest in the context of Parkinson's disease. Thus, the normal and pathological functioning of the basal ganglia (BG) cannot be fully elucidated without taking it into account. In this context, we analyzed the transfer of thalamic information into the BG by recording, in vivo, evoked responses at the output structure of the BG, the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), elicited by either electrical or optogenetic stimulation of the CM/Pf. We then investigated the BG components involved in these responses by analyzing evoked responses following specific optogenetic activation of the thalamostriatal, thalamosubthalamic, or thalamonigral pathways. Both electrical and optogenetic activation of the CM/Pf evoke complex responses in the SNr, composed of inhibition that can be preceded and/or followed by excitations. The inhibition and late excitation depend on the activation of trans-striatal pathways, whereas the early excitations involve the thalamosubthalamic and thalamonigral pathways. We also examined the impact of striatal cholinergic interneurons and dopaminergic afferents on the transfer of thalamic information within the BG. To this end, we recorded evoked responses in striatal projection neurons following electrical stimulation of the CM/Pf, with or without optogenetic inhibition of cholinergic interneurons (CINs). This will allow us to determine how CINs are involved in the transfer of thalamic information within the BG.

W0688.text: PROCESSING OF THALAMIC INFORMATION THROUGH THE BASAL GANGLIA: IN VIVO ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL AND OPTOGENETIC APPROACHES. The medial/parafascicular (CM/Pf) nucleus of the thalamus has recently emerged as a key element of interest in the context of Parkinson's disease. Thus, the normal and pathological functioning of the basal ganglia (BG) cannot be fully elucidated without taking it into consideration. In this context, we analyzed the transfer of thalamic information into the BG by recording, in vivo, the evoked responses at the output structure of the BG, the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), either by electrical or optogenetic stimulation of the CM/Pf. Subsequently, we investigated the BG components involved in these responses by analyzing the evoked responses elicited by specific optogenetic activation of the thalamostriatal, thalamosubthalamic, or thalamonigral pathways. Both electrical and optogenetic activation of the CM/Pf evoke complex responses in the SNr, which are composed of an inhibition that can be preceded and/or followed by excitations. The inhibition and late excitation depend on the activation of trans-striatal pathways, whereas the initial excitations involve the thalamosubthalamic and thalamonigral pathways. We also examined the impact of striatal cholinergic interneurons and dopaminergic afferents on the transfer of thalamic information into the BG. We will then be able to determine how CINs are involved in the transfer of thalamic information within the BG.

W0691.text: Anatomical and functional characterization of the motor corticosubthalamic pathway in non-human primates: a study using optogenetics, electrophysiology, 3D-histology, and tractography. Implications for neuromodulation strategies in the treatment of Parkinson's disease. Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder. Motor symptoms initially respond well to dopaminergic medications. However, motor complications from these drugs eventually emerge. Some patients are then offered neurosurgical treatment via deep brain stimulation (DBS) and chronic stimulation of the Subthalamic Nucleus (STN). Several studies suggest that modulation of the motor corticosubthalamic tract explains at least part of the efficacy of STN DBS. Deepening the understanding of the mechanism of action of STN DBS for PD treatment should enable optimization of the safety/efficacy ratio of this procedure, which is administered to tens of thousands of patients worldwide. The primary objective of this thesis is to characterize the motor corticosubthalamic tract anatomically and functionally in non-human primates. The secondary objectives are: To enable direct visualization of the STN under stereotaxic conditions in non-human primates and Parkinsonian patients - To develop a methodology for characterizing any fiber tract between two anatomically distinct brain regions, both anatomically and functionally, in non-human primates - To formulate a control law for closed-loop optogenetic stimulation of the STN, in order to selectively suppress beta oscillations and test the hypothesis of their role in the emergence of motor symptoms in PD...

This lack of information stems, in part, from the particular anatomy of this pathway, which makes in vitro study of the cortico-NST synapse difficult. The use of optogenetics allowed us to circumvent this problem.

W0799.text: Involvement of descending serotonergic pathways in the control of nociception in Parkinson's disease. Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the loss of dopaminergic (DA) neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, which is accompanied by characteristic motor symptoms as well as non-motor symptoms such as pain, whose mechanisms are not yet fully understood. In addition to DA, other systems, such as the serotonergic (5-HT) system, can also be affected by PD. This system is fundamental in pain control, with its neurons projecting to the spinal cord (SC). We therefore hypothesize that pain in PD is linked to a disruption of pain modulation by descending 5-HT pathways. To test this, we used the 6-OHDA model of PD in mice. We show that dopaminergic (DA) depletion bilaterally lowers mechanical pain thresholds, induces an increase in nociceptive activity in the spinal dorsal horn (SDH), and specifically causes hyperactivity of nociceptive neurons within the SDH. Furthermore, it leads to an increase in the activity of 5-HT neurons in the nucleus raphe magnus (NRM) and an increase in 5-HT levels in the SC. To verify that the hypersensitivity observed in 6-OHDA mice is directly related to the increased 5-HT activity, we used 5-HTcre transgenic mice and optogenetic techniques to specifically inhibit the descending 5-HT pathway. We thus show that inhibition of the 5-HT pathway allows for a partial restoration of pain sensitivity in 6-OHDA mice, as well as a decrease in nociceptive activity in the SDH. This restoration can be mimicked by intrathecal injection of 5-HT2a and 5-HT3 receptor antagonists. All of this indicates that DA depletion increases the activity of NRM 5-HT neurons, inducing spinal hyperexcitability associated with pain hypersensitivity. These results reveal a facilitatory role of 5-HT following DA depletion, whereas in naïve mice, the descending 5-HT pathway has been shown to inhibit pain, suggesting that the role of 5-HT in nociception control changes depending on the activity level of its neurons. We therefore investigated the role of the level of 5-HT pathway stimulation on nociception. We show that inhibition of 5-HT pathways reduces paw withdrawal thresholds and increases the activity of nociceptive neurons in the SDH, revealing a tonic anti-nociceptive role of the 5-HT pathway under normal conditions. Subsequently, we activated the 5-HT pathways using different optogenetic and chemogenetic protocols. We confirmed with optogenetics that short-term stimulation of 5-HT neurons is analgesic, whereas longer stimulations are pro-algesic. Chemogenetic experiments also suggest that different concentrations of DCZ lead to opposite control of pain, but additional experiments are needed to consolidate these results. However, all of this supports the hypothesis that the activity level of 5-HT neurons regulates their effect on nociceptive transmission. Finally, we explored the spinal 5-HT receptors involved and showed that the analgesic effect is mediated by 5-HT2a and 5-HTc receptors on local interneurons, while the hyperalgesic effect requires the recruitment of 5-HT3 receptors. In conclusion, this work demonstrates that (1) the activity level of 5-HT neurons is a crucial indicator of 5-HT control of pain, ranging from analgesia to hyperalgesia, and that (2) the loss of DA neurons leads to an increase in the activity of the descending 5-HT pathway, inducing nociceptive hypersensitivity linked to spinal 5-HT2a/5-HT3 receptors. This opens the way to exploring the use of 5-HT antagonists in the potential treatment of chronic pain in PD and the use of 5-HT neuron activity as an indicator of pathological pain.

W0800.text: Network dynamics of basal ganglia circuits in normal and parkinsonian conditions. The basal ganglia (BG) circuits are involved in various functions ranging from motor control to cognitive/motivational processes. The loss of dopamine (DA) in these circuits triggers Parkinson's disease (PD), characterized by devastating motor deficits known as akinisia and bradykinesia. In addition to DA depletion, PD patients exhibit early serotonergic (5-HT) alterations in the BG nuclei. 5-HT modulates BG circuit activity by acting on a wide variety of 5-HT receptor subtypes. Among them, the 5-HT2A receptor is expressed in the motor and associative/limbic territories of the BG nuclei and is involved in the regulation of motor, automatic, executive, and cognitive functions. Furthermore, it has been shown that 5-HT2A receptors may play a role in diseases associated with BG dysfunction, such as PD. However, precise information on the role of 5-HT2A receptors in these circuits is still lacking. Therefore, in the first part of my PhD project, we investigated the contribution of these receptors to the dynamic response of the BG output nuclei to the motor and prefrontal (mPF) cortical areas. To evaluate the effect of 5-HT2A receptor activation or blockade, we performed in vivo extracellular recordings from lateral and medial neurons of the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), combined with electrical stimulation of the motor or medial prefrontal cortex. The results showed a topography-dependent dissociation in the effects induced by TCB-2, a 5-HT2A agonist. TCB-2 specifically increased the activity of medial SNr neurons and acted on the processing of cortical information from the mPF via the direct striato-nigral pathway. These results provide evidence for the specific signature of 5-HT2A receptors in the dynamic regulation of BG circuits. In the second part of my doctoral work, we focused on BG dynamics under pathological conditions. At the early stage of PD, administration of the DA precursor L-DOPA reduces symptoms by improving movement execution but rapidly triggers abnormal and involuntary movements known as L-DOPA-induced dyskinesias (LID). LID are highly disabling and refractory to other pharmacological treatments. It is therefore fundamental to understand the neuronal mechanisms underlying LID in order to develop new therapeutic strategies. Recent studies have shown that LID are caused by aberrant neuronal activity in the striatum; however, it remains unknown how this activity affects BG circuits. Moreover, it is known that arky pallidal neurons of the GPe (Arky-GPe) directly form a negative feedback loop to the striatum, controlling action inhibition under normal conditions. Since this activity under pathological conditions remains unknown, this project aimed to characterize the changes in Arky-GPe activity across different stages: healthy state, PD, and LID. In this work, we used fiber photometry and miniscope methods to measure and track in vivo the calcium activity of the target neurons. After characterizing their activity changes, we tested their causal contribution to the generation of LID. To this end, we directly manipulated these neurons using optogenetic activation methods and observed a decrease in dyskinesia severity and a restoration of pseudo-normal motor behavior. These results pave the way for understanding the complex mechanisms involved in the genesis and maintenance of LID, an essential step for designing new therapeutic targets.

W0801.text: Subtype-specific inhibitory neuron generation enables psychiatric disorder neuronal activity screening. This study aims to induce efficient subtype-specific neuronal differentiation from human induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells, with the goal of analyzing the pathology of psychiatric disorders and performing drug screening. Furthermore, it seeks to establish an experimental system that can easily monitor neuronal activity in vitro. The principal investigator has successfully constructed a gene introduction system that induces subtype-specific neurons from iPS cells derived from patients with schizophrenia, neurodevelopmental disorders, and Alzheimer's disease. Additionally, a system that measures neuronal activity as optical readouts in response to optogenetically induced neuronal activity has been applied to iPS cell-derived neurons. This enables the measurement of synaptic formation capacity and neuronal activity capacity in neurons derived from patients with these disorders.
